China, the European Union and the United States are expected to remain the main drivers of EV battery deployment, but their combined share is set to decline over the coming years as deployment in EMDEs grows. In the STEPS, the share of EMDEs in global EV battery deployment rises from around 6% in 2025 to about 15% by 2035, driven primarily by EV uptake in Southeast Asia, India and Latin America. In contrast, the United States sees the sharpest decline in share under the CPS, falling from around 10% in 2025 to less than 5% in both 2030 and 2035, reflecting slower growth relative to other markets.

### Recycling will remain dominated by production scrap until end‑of‑life batteries take the lead in the mid‑2030s

Battery recycling is crucial for the long‑term sustainability of the battery industry and is likely to become an important future source of critical minerals, strengthening battery supply chain security and resilience. Today, recycling already plays an important role in supporting the battery value chain, primarily through the recovery of production scrap generated during the manufacturing of battery cells and components. However, beyond this, the contribution of recycling to meeting battery critical mineral needs still remains limited.

Deployment of EVs and battery storage systems – together representing around 90% of today’s lithium‑ion battery market – accelerated rapidly from 2020 onwards. Between 2020 and 2025, total lithium‑ion battery deployment across all applications increased more than sixfold and it continues to climb. The associated surge in battery production has driven up demand for critical minerals such as lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite.

The availability of end‑of‑life batteries for recycling has not increased at the same pace. Nearly all batteries deployed in EVs and stationary storage systems over the past few years remain in use today and most of them will operate until the mid-2030s, and potentially longer. In practical terms, this creates a structural time lag – roughly 15 years – between the growth in EV battery demand and the moment when comparable volumes of these batteries start reaching end of life and become available for recycling.

China has a strong position in access to end‑of‑life batteries, reflecting its status as the world’s largest battery producer and EV market, and it hosts over 85% of global recycling capacity.9 Some recyclers – notably Brunp, the CATL‑affiliated recycling subsidiary – benefit from direct links to major battery manufacturers, giving them preferential access to production scrap and ensuring steady feedstock volumes. However, others face difficulties in securing sufficient material feedstock, as recycling capacity is currently largely in excess compared to available feedstock globally.

Until recently, imports of black mass – a concentrated mixture of the metals originally contained in a lithium-ion battery – were banned in China. This changed in August 2025, when imports of high‑grade black mass were permitted. Import tariffs were also reduced at the start of 2026. While the short‑term impact has been limited, this policy shift could have significant medium‑term implications. In particular, part of the black mass produced outside China may increasingly be sent to Chinese facilities for recycling, attracted by the country’s available recycling capacity, expertise and lower processing costs. Nevertheless, this will also depend on regulations elsewhere, which could limit this flow.

At the same time, battery chemistry preference is shifting towards more affordable options, such as lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, while interest in sodium-ion batteries is growing. This poses challenges for recycling businesses relying on the economic value of the recovered critical minerals, potentially requiring different business models and devoted regulations to ensure that end‑of‑life batteries are properly collected and processed.

Toll-based models, in which the recycler is paid for the recycling service and the customer maintains ownership of the recycled materials, is an alternative approach. This model can be particularly effective when combined with policies that assign responsibility for end‑of‑life batteries to automakers or battery manufacturers, such as under the EU battery regulation or as recently introduced in China. Under such conditions, the main economic driver shifts away from the profit earned from selling recovered minerals – which may be insufficient for lower‑value chemistries – and towards the savings associated with recycling compared with the cost of disposing of used batteries. This can reduce price volatility in recycling services and make recycling economically viable even when the recycling process itself is not profitable on a standalone basis, supporting the role of recycling in making the lithium-ion battery supply chain more resilient while reducing their environmental impact.

### Future flows of used EVs, batteries and recycling feedstock are uncertain and will shape the recycling market

Prices for used EV batteries have fallen sharply in recent years, mirroring declines in new lithium‑ion battery prices and critical minerals. Historically, the price of used EV batteries has been particularly high, due to both inventories and the number of transactions being very limited. As flows of used and end-of-life EV batteries start to increase, prices are falling sharply, which over time will increase available material feedstock for recyclers, as well as opening up opportunities for battery reuse.

The used and end-of-life EV battery markets are still at an early stage, and future market dynamics are still to be defined. For example, in the second half of 2025 critical mineral prices began to rise again, while used EV battery prices in Europe and North America continued to fall. If this disconnection continues in the future, it might indicate that used EV batteries could be priced as a function of what downstream markets are willing to pay for reusing them, rather than as inventories of raw materials.

EV battery reuse, for example for energy storage applications, remains challenging. This is because of the safety and warranty requirements for second‑life applications, uncertainty in remaining lifetime, falling prices for new batteries that reduce the economic attractiveness of repurposing, costs of dismantling and repurposing safely used EV battery packs, and the transfer of responsibility for safety, liability, regulatory compliance and end‑of‑life management to the repurposer.

By contrast, the second‑hand EV market is expanding rapidly, and reselling, repairing or refurbishing used vehicles currently generates higher profits than dismantling them for parts. As a result, the batteries inside these vehicles continue to operate for several more years, including in different markets and regions from those where the vehicles were originally sold.

This trend could have important implications for future battery recycling markets, particularly in higher‑income regions such as Europe and North America. A share of the volumes initially expected to become available for recycling may materialise later than previously anticipated, and in different locations. Although recycling will strengthen the resilience of battery supply chains in these markets once sufficient batteries reach end‑of‑life, the growth of second‑hand EV markets may reduce feedstock availability. This could require a recalibration of expectations regarding the contribution of recycling to domestic critical mineral supplies in the coming years.

# Unlocking Supply Chains for Localizing Electric Vehicle Battery Production in India

This study aims to highlight the key supply chain barriers in localizing electric vehicle (EV) battery cell manufacturing in India. It summarizes consultations with 12 companies working on battery cell and equipment manufacturing, as well as experts and policy-makers, to determine the crucial challenges and opportunities in localizing battery manufacturing. The report also assesses trade and geopolitical risks and provides targeted policy recommendations to government agencies.

India has aspirations to become a prominent player in the global battery industry. The national government’s launch of the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage (PLI-ACC scheme) in 2021 reflects the country’s desire to indigenize battery manufacturing. This aspiration is driven by several priorities such as bolstering energy security, promoting local value addition, and accelerating transport electrification and stationary storage deployment. However, to truly capture value across the battery supply chain, India will need to pursue backward integration with the high-value cell components segment as well as equipment manufacturing. Hence, there is a strategic imperative to identify the barriers to localizing the supply chain and recalibrate India’s industrial and trade policies to build a competitive battery ecosystem.

India has the potential to add value across the global battery supply chain. Its chemical sector expertise; technological prowess; favourable trade and geopolitical relations; and growing network of free trade agreements with mineral-rich countries offer several opportunities. As the fourth-largest manufacturer of automobiles, the transition from internal combustion engines to electric vehicles (EVs) provides a significant economic opportunity if India is able to indigenize battery manufacturing.

Based on the analysis undertaken in this report, we recommend that the government focuses on maximizing India’s comparative advantages in the battery supply chains, through the following steps:

* India should prioritize the localization of specific battery components such as synthetic anodes, electrolytes, and cell casings and pouches, through supportive regulations and trade and industrial policies. The presence of domestic suppliers, high cost competitiveness, and low intellectual property and tech reliance create an opportunity for India to scale up its production.
* The government should also incentivize the development of domestic cathodes since these are the highest-value components in a cell. Although India’s technology-agnostic approach can help build domestic capabilities for different battery types, it should prioritize the development of lithium ferro phosphate (LFP) cathodes, as they are lower cost and more suitable for India’s climatic conditions. The adoption of LFP cathodes can offset the need for increased imports of critical minerals such as cobalt and nickel.
* The government should support research and development efforts and incentivize commercialization of the next generation of battery technologies, such as sodium-ion and solid-state, to seize potential opportunities created by the next evolution of the battery industry.
* India must adopt clearer environmental, social, and government guidelines and targets, as well as establish robust reporting frameworks to enhance the export competitiveness of domestic battery companies.
* Increased public investment in setting up cell fabrication and testing centres with trained workers is essential to validate the quality of raw materials, components, and equipment.
* The government should incentivize a circular economy ecosystem by enabling the recycling of end-of-life batteries and improving the collection efficiency of used batteries.
* The government also needs to prioritize the localization of critical equipment used in cell manufacturing through technology partnerships and trade agreements with key allies.

Nandan Dawda and Veer Puri, “India’s Critical Minerals Challenge in the Electric Mobility Era,” ORF Occasional Paper No. 560, Observer Research Foundation, July 2026.

Over two million electric vehicles (EV) were sold in India in 2024, a 27-percent increase from the previous year.[1] This uptake is part of a multi-fuel plan—encompassing compressed natural gas (CNG), hydrogen fuel cells, and biofuels—to address various aspects of India's complicated transportation environment.

Strong legislative frameworks and fast-growing infrastructure have accelerated the growth of the Indian EV sector and put the country on track to achieve its ambitious target of 30 percent EV penetration by 2030.[2] The number of public EV charging points is expected to reach 3.9 million in 2030, and oil companies have also pledged to install 22,000 charging stations in prominent cities and on national roads.[3] At the same time, Indian EV businesses attracted US$1 billion in funding from venture capital, private equity, and commercial bank avenues in 2024.[4] The push to deploy 10,000 electric buses under the PM Electric Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement (PM E-DRIVE) plan has further boosted the EV sector; 3,834 units were in operation as of 2024.[5]

However, India’s electric mobility aspirations face a geopolitical hurdle. While EV sales are increasing, supply chain fragility is a significant risk. In India, the clean energy transition is primarily dependent on a single external player: China. With a 100-percent import dependency on lithium, cobalt and nickel,[6] and China controlling over 90 percent of international processing of rare-earth elements,[7] India’s critical minerals supply is at risk of overreliance on China.

This dependency is a matter of national security. Historically, supply chains have been used as geopolitical leverage, as seen in Japan’s rare-earth embargo in 2010.[8] More recently, China’s restriction on exports of critical minerals, such as graphite and antimony, in 2023-24 has already led to market disruptions, with 35 Indian importers declaring force majeure over supply disruptions.[9]

Global trade dynamics are heightening this risk. As the United States (US) and the European Union (EU) continue to diversify their supply chains through alliances such as the Minerals Security Partnership (MSP),[10] the global market is fragmenting. India’s overreliance on external supply chains makes the domestic manufacturing sector vulnerable to border tensions and tariff changes. Its success in overcoming its dependence on Chinese-controlled critical mineral supply chains will be key to its overall energy transition. Enabling a strong energy transition is therefore a strategic mandate that will ensure the country does not become susceptible to shifts in global power dynamics.

Over the past decade or so, India has enacted specific policies to further its sustainable mobility goals (see Figure 1). Each policy has focused on translating these goals into market adoption and on developing a domestic supply chain.

In 2013, India adopted the National Electric Mobility Mission Plan, its first long-term vision on sustainable mobility. Two years later, in April 2015, the government began Phase I of the Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid &) Electric Vehicles (FAME I) project with an investment of INR 5.29 billion (~US$57 million).[11] FAME I promoted the purchase of some 280,000 EVs[12] and approved 520 charging stations (though only 452 were installed).[13] This was a beta phase to enable manufacturers to adapt to updated homologation standards and provide data to the transportation agencies on operational costs.

Figure 1: India’s EV Policies

Source: Authors’ own

Building on these insights, FAME II was launched in April 2019 with an outlay of INR 100 billion (US$1.20 billion).[14] FAME II promoted the use of advanced-chemistry cell batteries, thereby necessitating a shift away from lead-acid technologies.[15] It aimed to support 1 million e-two-wheelers, 500,000 e-three-wheelers, 55,000 e-four-wheelers, and 7,000 e-buses, as well as the requisite public charging infrastructure.[16] By March 2024, the initiative had subsidised approximately 1.62 million EVs, most of which were e-two-wheelers in tier-2 and tier-3 cities due to their low total ownership costs.[17] However, the scheme’s Phased Manufacturing Programme (PMP) localisation requirements[18] proved difficult to implement, and many manufacturers struggled to meet the domestic value addition thresholds required to qualify for subsidies.

In September 2024, the government greenlit the Prime Minister Electric Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement (PM E-DRIVE) initiative, committing INR 109 billion (US$1.3 billion) over two years.[19] PM E-DRIVE allocates INR 43.91 billion (US$526 million) to purchase 14,028 e-buses in key cities and INR 20 billion (US$240 million) to build public charging infrastructure, with a target of 22,100 fast charging points for four-wheelers and over 48,000 points for two- and three-wheelers.[20] Additionally, it allocates INR 7.80 billion (US$93 million) to upgrade and modernise the Ministry of Heavy Industries' testing agencies, including the facilities under the National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP), so as to equip them with the capacity to evaluate and certify new and emerging EV technologies.[21]

On the supply side, the production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for the automotive sector, approved in 2021 with an INR 259.38-billion (US$3.1 billion) budget,[22] aimed to achieve cost competitiveness through innovative technologies. The initiative provided sales-value-linked incentives of up to 18 percent for battery-electric and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles and components.[23] The government also approved the ACC-PLI scheme in May 2021 under the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage, committing INR 181 billion (US$2.16 billion) over five years to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity, with firms required to scale domestic value addition from 25 percent within two years to 60 percent within five.[24] As of late 2025, the project has received pledged investments of over INR 350 billion (US$4.2 billion), with tier-1 suppliers scaling up manufacturing capacity for critical components such as motors and cells.[25]

These policies facilitated notable growth in India’s EV sector between 2015 and 2025 (see Figure 2); by the end of FY2025, cumulative registered EVs exceeded 6.16 million.[26]

India's EV market is growing rapidly, with a projected strong demand for batteries. The lithium-ion battery market is projected to grow from 10.8 GWh in 2022 to 160.3 GWh by 2030,[29] spurred by an expected rapid adoption of electric two- and three-wheelers. This projected growth trajectory will require substantial secure access to critical minerals. According to NITI Aayog, producing 100 GWh of lithium-ion batteries by 2030 will require around 193,000 tonnes of cathode active material and 98,000 tonnes of anode active material per year, in addition to large quantities of copper, lithium, and aluminium.[30] These figures are based on an assumed battery chemistry mix of 60 percent lithium iron phosphate, 25 percent nickel manganese cobalt, and 15 percent lithium cobalt oxide. The actual quantities needed may vary depending on which battery chemistries are most widely used at the time, though other analyses broadly support this scale of demand.[31] Given India's EV targets, securing a steady supply of these minerals within a short timeframe is vital, as any supply chain disruptions can slow down the country's planned energy transition.

If India achieves its 30 percent EV sales target by 2030, it can create a INR 25.05-trillion (US$300 billion) local market for batteries.[32] The demand for certain critical minerals used in EV and energy storage applications is poised to increase under current technological assumptions. Most of India’s requirements for nickel, cobalt, and lithium are currently met through imports.[33] However, supply chain limitations and geopolitical susceptibility mean India must ensure mineral security.

India’s reliance on imports is substantial. India is entirely import-dependent for lithium, cobalt, and nickel, the three minerals most central to its battery manufacturing ambitions, and imports over 90 percent of its copper requirements and 60 percent of its natural graphite demand.[34] China is at the heart of this dependency: it accounts for over 80 percent of India's lithium imports, dominates the global processing of cobalt and nickel, and supplies the overwhelming majority of India’s battery-grade graphite.[35] India’s critical mineral import bill reflects this exposure, having more than doubled from US$3.03 billion in 2020-21 to US$8.01 billion in 2023-24, while critical mineral exports fell from US$5 billion to US$3.99 billion over the same period, widening the trade imbalance.[36] A February 2026 NITI Aayog assessment found that demand for battery-linked minerals under a net-zero scenario will be 51 percent higher than under current policy, meaning the concentration of supply in Chinese hands is not a temporary vulnerability but a structural one that will only intensify as India scales its energy transition.[37]

The National Critical Minerals Mission (NCMM), which aims to address supply chain and technology constraints that impact domestic mineral security, has been provided INR 343 billion (US$4.1 billion) in funding over a seven-year period, of which INR 163 billion (US$1.95 billion) is government spending and INR 180 billion (US$2.15 billion) is expected to be invested by public sector undertakings.[38] The NCMM aims to conduct 1,200 domestic exploration projects, purchase 50 mining sites globally by 2030-31, and focus on domestic production of at least 15 core critical minerals, with national stockpiles of at least five minerals. To tackle its structural import dependency, India has taken strategic diversification measures, including partnering with Argentina on five lithium exploration blocks[39] and with Australia for a critical minerals investment.[40] Additionally, the discovery of potential lithium reserves in Jammu and Kashmir is also promising.[41]

The current growth trajectory of EVs indicates that manageable mineral needs are scaling to industrial levels, requiring a massive realignment in India’s resource security policies, international partnerships, and domestic production capabilities by 2030. However, India’s lithium refining capability is still in its early stages. Although one company has constructed and begun operating the country’s first battery-grade lithium refinery (with a 1,000 TPA capacity),[42] the main challenge is developing domestic processing capacity to prepare raw materials to produce battery-ready components for India’s electric mobility transition.

EVs need six times as many minerals as traditional cars.[43] Notably, critical raw materials account for 60 percent of EV battery manufacturing costs.[44] The EV sector relies on lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, and graphite, which form the backbone of advanced battery technologies. Additionally, aluminium, copper, steel, and rare-earth elements are necessary to ensure performance, safety, and durability.

India’s electric mobility shift depends not only on the country’s vehicle production capacity and charging infrastructure but also, more fundamentally, on the availability, processing, and financing of critical minerals and battery materials. While lithium-ion batteries require a specific set of materials—lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, manganese, copper, aluminium, and iron—the strategic risk for India lies in the uneven domestic availability, processing capacity, and import dependence in key areas of the battery value chain.

This section presents a systems-level evaluation of the critical mineral system in India, considering geological availability, processing and refining capacity, material flow potential (recycling), and financing requirements. Rather than focusing on the geological availability of minerals, this evaluation places greater emphasis on the positioning of the value chain and the security of materials.

India has a large geological inventory of minerals important to the production of EV batteries, including aluminium (bauxite), iron ore, manganese, and copper (see Table 2 for a summary of the domestic availability and development status of important battery minerals). These minerals are mined in commercial quantities and have a well-established mining and refining infrastructure. India’s manganese ore deposits are estimated at around 503.6 million tonnes, meaning the country is well placed to produce manganese-based cathode materials.[53] Iron and aluminium also have well-established domestic mining and processing infrastructure.[54]

Conversely, the domestic supply of electrochemically important minerals, such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and battery-grade graphite, remains limited. In February 2023, the Geological Survey of India announced the discovery of 5.9 million tonnes of inferred lithium deposits (G3 category) in the Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir.[55] Although this is a substantial find, it is still in the early stages of exploration and needs further evaluation, feasibility studies, and environmental approvals before commercial production can be considered.

India has only a few cobalt and nickel deposits, mostly found alongside copper deposits in Odisha, Jharkhand, Manipur, and Nagaland. Government estimates have categorised these deposits as small and not adequate for large-scale battery production.[56] Graphite deposits are found across various states, but the domestic capacity for purified natural or artificial graphite for lithium-ion batteries is still small.[57]

The availability of mineral deposits affects future prospects; however, the immediate pressing issue for India is the capacity to process and refine battery-grade materials to produce products. India has established aluminium and copper refining industries, with vertically-integrated operations from mine to metal.[63] At the same time, it lacks lithium refining capacity; therefore, the majority of its lithium needs are met through imports of lithium carbonate or hydroxide.[64] In addition, cobalt and nickel have very limited refining capacity to produce battery-grade intermediates; thus, India relies on imported cathode active materials and anode materials.[65]

While a number of companies have announced plans to produce cathode active materials, process battery-grade graphite, and manufacture electrolyte, these efforts are still only at the pilot or limited early commercial production levels.[66] These deficiencies explain why some high-value segments of the battery value chain remain dependent on imports, despite recent government interventions aimed at encouraging localisation.

Analysis of the supply chain, including trade data and a review of policies, indicates that lithium compounds, battery-grade graphite, cobalt intermediates and lithium-ion cells are largely imported from East Asia (China, South Korea, and Japan).[77]

While India has limited processing capacity for battery cathode and anode materials to manufacture cells, it has a lower import dependence for battery pack assembly.

A critical challenge for India is the lack of reliable data on many minerals.[78] India has an estimated substantial quantity of lithium, although the global average for the convertibility of inferred mineral resources (such as lithium into usable, extractable quantities of reserve) is negligible.[79] Also, domestically available sources of lithium will allow the country to meet either its projected supply or demand for lithium to support its rapidly growing EV fleet.[80] This emphasises the need for a secondary lithium supply through the recycling of EV batteries.

Renewably recovered lithium from recycled lithium-ion batteries can be expected to have a recovery rate over 90 percent for cobalt and nickel, 70 percent for lithium, and 80 percent for copper and aluminium as recycling technologies continue to evolve.[81] India is expected to experience rapid EV growth in the 2020s, leading to a corresponding increase in the number of EV batteries retired after 2030.[82]

Financing critical minerals and batteries is challenging, as significant capital is required to build processing, refining, and recycling facilities, amidst long development timelines and market volatility.[83] Consequently, it is difficult to attract private sector investments in most upstream and midstream battery value chain processes; however, there are strong demand increases in the downstream EV automotive industry.[84],[85] The processing/refining/recycling sectors of lithium-ion batteries are among the most constrained due to long build times, volatility in commodity prices, and uncertainty in demand from suppliers. Given these factors, additional financing will be required, as private-sector financing is unlikely to be sufficient until the commercial viability of each segment's products has been determined.

Tools like blended finance mechanisms[86] (the use of public funds, concessional finance, and private capital) support the first two segments of the value chain early, which will allow potential private-sector participation once commercial viability has been demonstrated.[87]

China has disproportionate control over entire essential supply chains for critical minerals, spanning from resource extraction and processing to capital deployment abroad, export controls, and overall vertical integration.[88] China thus enjoys an extraordinary advantage in determining the trajectory of the global transition to sustainable transportation.

Extensive Processing and Extraction Capacity: China’s dominance stems from its extensive control over initial mining and, most importantly, the subsequent processing of minerals needed for advanced EV battery systems. China accounts for 70 percent of the global rare earth elements mining capacity. It also controls 90 percent of the world’s rare-earth processing and refining capacity,[89] which is essential to produce high-performance permanent magnets used in EV powertrains, wind energy production, and advanced electronic devices.

Beyond rare earths, China’s control also extends over a considerable share of the refining capacity of the other essential metals. In 2024, China accounted for around 68 percent of global nickel refining capacity, 65 percent of lithium chemical processing, 74 percent of cobalt refining, and 44 percent of copper refining, reinforcing its strategic control over key inputs required for batteries, electric vehicles, and clean energy technologies.[90] The Chinese monopoly thus poses a dilemma for India: even if it extracts mineral resources from other countries, it will still have to depend on China for processing.[91]

Systematic International Investment and Upstream Security: China has made enormous investments in mineral-rich countries to meet its long-term domestic needs.[92] Aided by credit, direct purchases, and state-financed industrial projects, Chinese companies have taken control of the majority of mining and processing operations in Congo (cobalt), Indonesia (nickel), Argentina (lithium), and Peru (copper).[93] These strategic investments have enabled China to not only secure a steady supply of critical minerals but also influence upstream resource extraction abroad, shaping the order of international trade flows.

Geopolitical Leverage through Export Control: China’s domination of the global rare-earths market and its end-to-end control of the supply chain have enabled it to wield geopolitical influence by resorting to export curbs[94],[95] and introducing licensing conditions and volume quotas. By restricting exports, China has gained control over the pricing of rare minerals and in dealings with countries that depend on it for refined mineral supply. China’s use of export limitations as a geo-economics tool has allowed it to frequently shock the international market, thereby increasing its bargaining power in bilateral and multilateral trade relations.[96]

Comprehensive Vertical Integration and Technical Proficiency: China has created an extensive, vertically integrated industrial ecosystem covering the entire value chain, from raw mineral procurement and cutting-edge battery-cell fabrication to material recycling.[97] Such end-to-end control enables Chinese companies to capture the value created at each step of the supply chain, including mining, chemical refining, component and alloy manufacturing, and the production of advanced cathode and anode materials. Built over the years through targeted investments backed by precise policies, scale of operations, technical know-how, and complete regulatory support, China’s domination of the global rare earths market is difficult for other countries to replicate in a short period,[98] even those countries with abundant mineral resources. Without China’s specialised processing capabilities, the raw materials reserves in these countries will remain severely underleveraged.

Systemic Risk Implications for Global EV Deployment: China’s dominance of the critical mineral supply network has created systemic vulnerabilities for the global EV market.[99] The overdependence on China’s refining infrastructure has created a structural vulnerability, in which even minor events, such as sudden regulatory changes, intensified export restrictions, or rising geopolitical tensions, could trigger severe global supply bottlenecks.[100] Moreover, China’s export controls allow it to dictate trade terms to the extent that it can jeopardise the energy security of dependent nations.

The enormous scale of investment required to establish specialised refineries aligned with domestic and international environmental regulations, while overcoming technological barriers, poses a challenge to emerging market players seeking to take on China’s position. For the global EV industry and climate action, China’s material concentration poses an underlying strategic risk and presents an urgent need to build robust, geographically diversified supply chains. Solving this imbalance calls for coordinated international policies, targeted incentives for the decentralisation of refining capacity, and continued investments in alternative resource technologies and state-of-the-art recycling infrastructure.

India must formulate a comprehensive, multifaceted strategy (see Figure 3) to reduce its dependence on China.[101] It can adopt a cohesive national action plan based on the following proposed four-pillar strategic framework that focuses on: (i) developing an upstream resource-secure environment; (ii) establishing a robust domestic industrial base with strong technological capabilities; (iii) creating the conditions for and gaining access to a supportive policy and commercial ecosystem; and (iv) leveraging international diplomacy to build resilient global partnerships.

The NCMM, introduced in 2025, aims to secure and diversify sources of critical minerals. The mission entails exploring and developing all available domestic sources and securing assured access through acquisition or long-term supply agreements with like-minded countries.[102] Given the geopolitical sensitivities of critical minerals and their concentrated distribution worldwide, it will be imperative for India to diversify its sources of essential minerals internationally while strategically stockpiling the necessary metals.

Enhancing domestic mining and refining capacity: India must bolster domestic capabilities in the exploration, extraction, and refining of critical minerals to reduce its reliance on imports. Recent governmental policies, including the NCMM, have helped make strides toward boosting domestic capabilities; however, long-standing regulatory and institutional constraints continue to restrict the development of critical minerals, both in scale and speed.

Historically, India has had low exploration intensity for critical minerals due to the predominance of public-sector agencies (such as the Geological Survey of India) in exploration, coupled with limited private-sector participation.[103] The appetite for risk and innovation has been constrained by the lack of private-sector involvement; the potential for exploring long-gestation/high-risk critical minerals (such as lithium and rare-earth elements) is also limited. Indeed, restricted access to mineral blocks, uncertainty regarding post-discovery mining rights, and a lack of risk-sharing mechanisms will dissuade private investment in greenfield exploration.[104]

These challenges are compounded by complex regulations. Due to the different laws governing mining in India, all projects require multiple types of permissions, including environmental, forest, and wildlife clearances. While these legal protections are valid, the fragmented and excessively lengthy approval processes and timelines often cause project uncertainty, particularly amidst volatility in the global critical minerals marketplace.[105] Importantly, the government has recognised the need for more efficient and predictable clearance processes, while emphasising the need not to compromise on environmental standards.[106]

Rare-earth elements and monazite-bearing sands are important to India's long-term critical mineral objectives, but are subject to specific regulatory constraints. Historically, rare-earth elements are categorised as either strategic or atomic. As such, there has been a restriction on private companies’ participation in the exploration and development of rare-earth elements, and competition among those allowed to explore.[107] In addition, monazite-bearing sands in southern India are located in coastal regulation zones where mining activities must comply with detailed environmental protections and stringent land-use restrictions.[108]

Addressing these constraints will require an approach that focuses on targeted legislative, legal, and regulatory reforms rather than generic deregulation. Priorities include: (i) creating new exploration incentives and risk-sharing measures to increase private sector participation in the exploration of critical minerals; (ii) creating greater certainty around the transition from exploration to mining leases; (iii) streamlining the environmental and forest clearance process through coordinated, time-bound approvals while still maintaining environmental safeguards; and (iv) clarifying the regulatory framework for rare-earth elements and coastal minerals to facilitate responsible private sector participation.

The development of technological partnerships is also critical to establishing environmentally responsible mining and processing. Currently, India lacks large-scale, low-impact technologies for separating rare earths or refining lithium; as a result, there are concerns about the environmental and social impacts associated with the extraction of critical minerals.[109] International collaboration and technology transfer through contributions from public sector institutions will help mitigate environmental risks and build domestic capacity more quickly.

By initiating these measures to develop stronger domestic mining and refining capacity, India will not only reduce its reliance on imports but also capture greater value, increase supply chain resilience, and create greater strategic autonomy in its transition to electric mobility.

Additionally, India must expand the NCMM’s objective of investing in the exploration and acquisition of critical mineral assets abroad. Australia has become a key supplier of lithium and rare earths by supporting companies like Lynas Corporation, the largest producer of rare earths outside China.[110] The US Inflation Reduction Act, which provides tax incentives for onshore refined/processed materials for battery production, can provide learnings for similar domestic policies that incentivise Indian refiners.[111] Such policies, coupled with the recent auctioning of critical mineral blocks, will also attract foreign investors, reducing India’s reliance on international markets and making it self-sufficient.[112]

Building International Alliances, Diversifying Import Sources: India has partnered with countries with abundant critical mineral reserves,[113] such as Argentina for lithium, Australia for rare-earth metals, and several African nations for cobalt and nickel.[114] These partnerships will simplify long-term offtake contracts, encourage Indian equity investments in foreign mineral development projects, and foster joint processing ventures.

India can learn from international collaborations to proactively broaden this approach. For instance, following China’s cessation of rare-earth exports in 2010,[115] Japan established partnerships with countries such as Vietnam, Australia, Malaysia, the US, and India,[116] which enabled it to reduce its reliance on Chinese imports from nearly 90 percent to about 60 percent.[117] Similarly, South Korea has partnered with Chile, Canada, and Indonesia to meet the needs of its domestic EV battery manufacturers.[118] The EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act has set diversification targets and mandated that all member states develop shared strategic stockpiles of these critical minerals.[119]

India needs to focus on creating a comprehensive ecosystem around the critical mineral value chain, from mining and refining to manufacturing components and developing advanced technologies. Targeted investment in research and development (R&D), the development of new technologies, the establishment of industrial clusters, and the incentivisation of manufacturing through the following measures will spur the development of indigenous production capabilities.

Expanding Vertical Integration through R&D, Manufacturing, and Urban Mining: China’s dominance of the EV industry is driven by its access to raw materials and minerals as well as the vertical integration of the entire supply chain into finished products—from refining raw material into cathodes, producing battery cells and components, and reclaiming residual materials through battery recycling operations. India must develop its technological and industrial strengths in a similar manner.

In addition to the PLI schemes to boost battery cell manufacturing, India must focus on R&D for next-generation battery chemistries (such as sodium-ion and solid-state batteries) and on improving lithium iron phosphate batteries.[120] It must also ramp up its ‘urban mining’ capabilities by nurturing a recycling ecosystem to extract lithium, cobalt, and nickel from used batteries.[121] Creating a supportive policy and industry environment that includes, among other things, mandatory extended producer responsibilities for battery manufacturers, financial incentives for establishing large-scale mechanical and hydrometallurgical recycling facilities, and PLIs to encourage private sector investments[122] can help India establish an urban mining ecosystem that fosters a circular supply chain, reducing its dependence on imported raw materials. Additionally, developing local networks for collecting waste materials and reverse supply chain networks to support consistent metal recovery is equally critical.

By learning from international experiences, such as that of Swedish battery firm Northvolt (now defunct)[123] and US firm Redwood Materials, which aims to reclaim over 95 percent of critical minerals from used batteries,[124] India’s emerging recycling industry can become a significant urban mining hub that meets its domestic needs.[125]

Accelerate R&D in Alternative Battery Chemistries: India will reduce its dependency on lithium-, cobalt-, and nickel-based global supply chains by accelerating the adoption of alternative battery chemistries and enhancing its domestic R&D capabilities.[126] Strategic investments in emerging battery technologies, such as sodium-ion batteries, advanced lithium iron phosphate, and solid-state chemistries, will enable India to shift from a dependence on supply chains that rely on rare minerals to ones that utilise more readily available raw materials.[127] India must encourage pilot-scale manufacturing of alternative chemistries by supporting domestic R&D through milestone-based grants, competitive funding sources, and tax incentives. Facilitating industry-academia collaborations and simplifying the regulatory process for testing new battery chemistries can help India achieve early breakthroughs in its quest for alternative chemistries. Similar policy measures in Europe and the US have spurred innovation in developing alternative battery chemistries, advancing from the experimental stage to pilot-scale deployment.

Build Midstream Processing ‘Islands’ with Non-Chinese Technology Partners: India’s collaborations with established international technology partners must extend to establishing domestic midstream processing hubs. India will benefit from strengthened industrial capacity for advanced smelting and refining. Active collaborations built on robust regulatory and financial conditions between Indian companies and technology licensors in Australia, Japan, South Korea, and the EU countries, which entail technology transfer while safeguarding foreign licensors’ intellectual property over sensitive technologies, can accelerate this effort. The Japan-Australia partnership to develop a processing facility that avoids reliance on China’s refining network showcases a successful, global-scale model that India can emulate.[128]

Healthy and robust regulatory, financial, and institutional mechanisms must undergird India’s long-term critical minerals strategy. A stable legislative framework, an efficient licensing system, clear environmental protection measures, a trained workforce, and financial tools to continually attract private investment are vital to such a strategy. Innovation, reduced administrative delays, and strong links between private companies, government agencies, and academic institutions through the following measures can accelerate India’s critical mineral project development and establish it as a credible international market for critical minerals.

Mobilising Blended Finance and De-Risking Private Investment: Mobilising blended finance and de-risking private investment are crucial to the successful implementation of India’s critical minerals strategy.[129] The supply chain requires massive up-front capital and long initial investment cycles to build refining and recycling facilities.[130] Mobilising private capital to develop large-scale projects requires public equity, concessional finance, guarantees, and blended finance tools. Establishing a National Critical Minerals Fund to encourage public and private investments in mineral assets abroad and building domestic refining capacity and recycling facilities can not only raise substantial funds, but also de-risk the market environment to attract private equity.[131]

Additional tools, including political risk insurance,[132] viability gap funding, and tax holidays for long-term projects, will further reduce investor risk. India can emulate the experience of the government-supported Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security, which has successfully deployed such tools to reduce the risks of foreign upstream investment by Japanese companies.[133]

Using Public Procurement and Demand Signals to Localise Value Chains: Public procurement by and clear demand signals from the government can effectively reduce the industry’s dependence on foreign suppliers.[134] By guaranteeing to buy locally produced EVs and battery products through specified procurement processes, the government can enable local manufacturers to invest in upstream processes, creating capacity to not only make batteries but also a supporting industrial complex that underpin these processes. Establishing a minimum local-sourcing threshold for battery components for public-sector vehicle fleets and creating preferential procurement opportunities for local battery manufacturers must be integral to such a strategy. The government could also provide time-bound procurement contracts that can expand in proportion to domestic manufacturing capabilities.

Strengthening Traceability, Certification, and ESG Standards: Building traceability, certification procedures, and ESG (environmental, social, and governance) reporting standards for India’s critical mineral supply chains are crucial for establishing a level of transparency, reducing dependence on the Chinese supply chain, and improving buyers’ confidence.[135] Building trust-based relationships with non-Chinese suppliers through a certified and transparent supply chain will also promote the ethical and responsible sourcing of critical minerals. The implementation of advanced digital traceability solutions, such as block chain and internet of things-enabled systems, can support the verification of the origin, transit, and processing paths of minerals.[136] As part of its efforts to establish a robust and environmentally-just critical mineral supply chain through disclosures for battery and component manufacturers, India must develop national certification standards for the responsible sourcing of minerals and provide financial assistance to implement traceability pilot projects.[137] The EU’s forthcoming due diligence regulations and the integration of digital traceability solutions by private operators aim to diversify its procurements from ESG-compliant supplier networks.[138] India can learn from this experience.

Accelerating Skill Development and Workforce Transition Programmes: Integrating upskilling courses into science and engineering curricula will help accelerate the growth of India’s mining, refining, manufacturing, and recycling sectors, and improve productivity. It will also minimise workforce disruptions during the transition from a traditional fossil-fuel economy to a clean-energy one.[139] Leading industrial entities can also introduce skilling and upskilling modules and apprenticeships as a corporate social responsibility offering to build an industry-ready skilled labour force, creating new job opportunities.

Upskilling is also critical to retain the current workforce as fossil fuel industries eventually adopt clean energy processes. This approach will ensure that India has a scalable workforce capable of actively contributing to achieving its clean energy targets.

Tactical Trade and Tariff Measures to Encourage Localisation: Trade and tariffs play a tactical role in developing localised battery manufacturing by localising the entire critical minerals value chain.[140] The time-bound use of tariffs, countervailing duties, and selective import surcharges on finished product components can give India’s domestic industry a competitive edge and enhance the national market capacity. Such tactical measures must be carefully calibrated, aligned with India’s World Trade Organization commitments, paired with transparent and phased domestic content requirements, and supported by clearly defined sunset clauses.[141] Such a phased tactical approach can increase domestic production without significantly distorting the existing market and provide a predictable signal for manufacturers to invest in capacity expansion.

Other countries are critical to India achieving its goal of diversifying its mineral trading partners and reducing its dependence on China. India has already sought to enhance its bilateral and multilateral relationships by developing strategic alliances and joint ventures, as well as through technology-sharing agreements and investments in each other’s mineral resources. India is also participating in global critical mineral alliances, such as the Minerals Security Partnership,[142] the Quad Critical and Emerging Technologies Working Group,[143] and the India-EU Trade and Technology Council,[144] which aim to diversify supply chains, strengthen mineral security, and promote responsible sourcing. Establishing stronger relationships with resource-rich countries, particularly Australia and those in Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia, will help India develop robust supply routes for minerals, gain access to advanced technologies for mineral exploration, and increase its ability to influence global mineral governance.[145]

Forge Regional and Plurilateral Partnerships: India must reinforce its strategic position in the global critical minerals landscape by actively pursuing foreign, regional, and plurilateral partnerships to strengthen its bargaining power and diversify supply chains. Leveraging diplomatic forums and multilateral initiatives can help India foster more resilient, cooperative resource networks. An Indo-Pacific Critical Minerals Partnership among India, Australia, Japan, and South Korea could serve as a crucial mechanism for coordinating upstream exploration, technology sharing, and strategic investments across the region.[146] India’s deeper engagement with the US-led Minerals Security Partnership (MSP)[147] will further align its priorities with those of the advanced economies and promote the supply of responsibly sourced minerals. Enhanced South-South cooperation with resource-rich countries in Africa and Latin America can allow for joint ventures, capacity-building programmes, and long-term offtake agreements. These arrangements can support the creation of shared stockpiles, cross-border pooled investments, and collaborative refining projects, enabling India to secure stable supply lines while contributing to a more diversified and equitable global minerals ecosystem.[148]

Policy Reforms, Incentives, and Diplomatic Engagement: Developing a resilient, competitive ecosystem for critical minerals requires effective policy reforms, targeted incentives, and strategic diplomatic engagement.[149] Robust, forward-looking policy frameworks attract investment, drive technological advancement, and provide regulatory clarity to industry stakeholders. India needs to rationalise procedures for mineral licensing and approvals, establish predictable, transparent regulatory pathways, and offer fiscal and non-fiscal incentives to fast-track domestic refining, processing, and battery manufacturing capabilities.[150] Integrating critical minerals into the country’s larger diplomatic and trade strategy is equally important, especially as global supply chains are increasingly securitised. To this end, the NCMM must be advanced to foster institutional coherence and long-term strategic planning.[151]

International experience underlines the significance of coordinated policy and diplomacy in securing mineral value chains. The EU’s strategic partnerships with resource-rich countries such as Namibia, Kazakhstan, and Canada have ensured stable access to raw materials vital for the green transition.[152] India's participation in plurilateral forums like the Quad, coupled with bilateral engagement with Australia, Argentina, and a host of African countries, can similarly provide a robust diplomatic framework to expand resource access, increase technology cooperation, and strengthen supply-chain resilience.[153]

India’s sustained progress in the energy transition, characterised by rapid EV adoption and scaled domestic manufacturing, parallels an unprecedented increase in global competition, including the securitisation of critical mineral supply chains. This paper has highlighted a strategic vulnerability: the endemic dependence of India’s emerging clean mobility sector on a value chain for mineral processing and refinement predominantly owned by other countries, particularly China. India’s required battery capacity is expected to grow exponentially by 2030, putting extraordinary pressure on sourcing mechanisms, refining throughput, and midstream value-addition capabilities. To navigate this high-stakes environment, India must transition to a holistic. foresight-driven resource security doctrine.

The strategic framework proposed in this paper provides a coherent national strategy to mitigate these vulnerabilities and unlock sustainable, long-term competitiveness: securing upstream assets through intensified domestic prospecting and strategic overseas acquisitions; developing sovereign industrial capacity by scaling domestic refinement and advanced cell manufacturing while speeding up recycling and ‘urban mining’ to build a circular economy for critical materials; establishing enabling ecosystems by promulgating clear regulatory standards, implementing blended finance mechanisms, and enforcing stringent ESG and traceability standards; and finally, leveraging mineral diplomacy through focused bilateral, regional, and plurilateral engagement with key resource-ri

## India Electric Vehicle Battery Manufacturing Market Trends and Insights

### Lithium-ion Battery Type to Dominate the Market

* India's electric vehicle (EV) battery manufacturing market is set for substantial growth, primarily fueled by the supremacy of lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries. Li-ion batteries, known for their superior energy density, extended life cycles, and enhanced performance, have become the go-to choice for EV manufacturers focused on delivering reliable and efficient vehicles.
* To bolster EV adoption and stimulate local EV battery manufacturing, the Indian government has rolled out a series of initiatives.
